name: A comparison over blanks is false; a comparison over an unknown is unknown
why: The sharpest distinction in the language, and the one an implementation loses by accident. A blank number reads as zero, so two blanks compare as `0 < 0` and the answer is a definite FALSE. But a comparison whose operand could not be worked out is neither true nor false, and a bare `<` on two nullables in C# answers false for both — which would make a rule keyed on 'is the balance below the threshold' fire on every record whose balance has not been computed yet.

cases.why: Both blank. FALSE, definitely — not unknown. Both fields read as zero, and zero is not less than zero. An implementation answering null here has confused an empty field with an unworkable figure.
And equal, definitely, for the same reason. Two blanks are two zeros.
Now the other kind of missing. The balance could not be worked out, so whether it is below the threshold is UNKNOWN — not false. This is the case the whole file is for.
Unknown on the right-hand side too.
`lt` and `gt` are therefore NOT each other's negation once an unknown is involved. Both are unknown rather than one being true.
Equality over an unknown is unknown as well. Two figures nobody could work out are not thereby equal.
The boundary is inclusive where the operator says so.
